title: Burns
summary: Cool a minor burn, cover it, and know which burns need 911.

blocks.text: **Call 911** if the burn is about the size of your palm or bigger, is white or charred (full-thickness), was caused by chemicals or electricity, the person breathed in smoke, there are signs of shock, or you are not sure how serious it is.

rows: Red, painful, a bit swollen. Only the top layer of skin.
White or blackened skin. It may be numb.

blocks.text: **Minor:** any first-degree burn, or a second-degree burn less than 2 to 3 inches wide. **Major:** third-degree burns, second-degree burns wider than 2 to 3 inches, or second-degree burns on the hands, feet, face, groin, buttocks or over a major joint.

items: Hold the burn under cool running water or soak it in cool water (not ice water). MedlinePlus says at least 5 to 30 minutes.
Cover it with a dry, sterile bandage or clean dressing.
Protect it from pressure and rubbing.
Ibuprofen or acetaminophen can ease pain and swelling (see the OTC medicines guide). Do not give aspirin to anyone under 19.
Make sure tetanus shots are up to date.
If clothing is on fire, have the person stop, drop and roll, then smother the flames with a thick coat, rug or blanket and pour water on them.
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the skin.
Check breathing. Start CPR if needed.
Cover the burn with a dry sterile bandage or clean cloth (a clean sheet for a large area).
Raise the burned part above heart level if you can.
To prevent shock, if there is no head, neck, back or leg injury, lay the person flat, raise their feet about 12 inches (30 cm), and cover them with a coat or blanket.
Watch breathing and pulse until help arrives.

blocks.text: Do not touch the person directly. Use a non-metallic object to separate them from the source first. Call 911 for any electrical or chemical burn.

items: Do not put ice, butter, oil, creams, sprays or home remedies on a severe burn.
Do not put a severe burn in cold water, since that can cause shock.
Do not break or pull off blisters or dead skin.
Do not breathe, blow or cough on the burn.
Do not give anything by mouth for a severe burn.

blocks.text: See a provider if a minor burn still hurts after 48 hours, and sooner for signs of infection: pus or drainage, fever, more pain, red streaks or swollen glands. Children, older adults and people with weak immune systems should be seen promptly.
